blocks.s: Furthermore, this devout man introduces three species of speculative contemplation. The first is called natural or physical: this seeks and inspects the Creator through the mirror of creatures, through whose consideration the philosophers knew God. The second he calls scholastic: this contemplates God through the mirror of the Scriptures and acquired wisdom. This is said to be useful and necessary; yet sometimes it accidentally impedes the influxions of celestial illuminations, when the soul is held captive through excessive occupation in Scriptures and lessons, and is thereby distanced from the fellowship of God and from interior colloquy — which, alas, happens frequently to many religious who study indiscreetly and do not extend knowledge to practice. The third he calls divinely infused: this contemplates God through the rays of wisdom poured from above, and divine droppings touching the highest portion of the soul — as was more fully said in the preceding book, article nineteen.
The devout Guigo writes many other useful things in his treatise, some of which may find a place below.

[REVIEW NEEDED — This rendering of De contemplatione, Liber Secundus (11 articles) was made for Still from the Latin of the Opera omnia XLI, 1912 Tournai edition. The two-column OCR interleaving in the source causes certain passages, especially in Articles V and VI, to be reconstructed from context. Article VI's opening attribution was lost in the column interleaving; the content follows from the surrounding text.]
